N01.code: BNSS applies: the FIR and investigation are from 2025, after 1 July 2024, so the charge-sheet is filed under s.193 BNSS and s.190 BNSS governs production of the accused. The rule is the same as under s.170 CrPC. If the alleged cheating took place after 1 July 2024, the offence is BNS s.318(4); before that date, IPC s.420.
N01.expected_answer: No. Section 190 BNSS (old s.170 CrPC) does not oblige the officer to arrest every accused when filing the charge-sheet. 'Custody' there only means presenting the accused before the court. If he has joined the investigation and there is no reason to think he will abscond or ignore summons, he need not be arrested. The magistrate cannot refuse to take the charge-sheet on record because the accused was not produced in custody; the ordinary course is to issue summons.

authorities.label: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1996/97)

N02.code: BNSS s.58(2) (old CrPC s.57) and Article 22(2) apply whatever the date. Even if the pills are found to be NDPS contraband, the NDPS Act (s.36A, s.52A) does not extend the 24-hour production limit.
N02.expected_answer: No. Under Article 22(2) of the Constitution and s.58(2) BNSS (old s.57/167 CrPC), every person arrested must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time of the journey. This is a non-derogable right. The police cannot detain anyone beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's remand order, regardless of the nature of the offence or whether investigation is complete. The NDPS Act does not override this requirement.

N03.expected_answer: Yes. A person is 'in custody' for s.439 CrPC once he physically appears before the court and submits to its jurisdiction and directions. Arrest by police is not needed. Having surrendered, he can apply for regular bail to the Sessions Court or the High Court, and the court can decide it. The BNSS equivalent of s.439 is s.483.

N04.code: CrPC s.167(2) read with UAPA s.43D(2) applies to an arrest before 1 July 2024. For an arrest from that date, BNSS s.187(3) is read with UAPA s.43D(2) to the same effect.
N04.expected_answer: No. Under the UAPA, only the Special Court (or, where no Special Court is designated, the Court of Session) can extend the investigation period from 90 to 180 days under s.43D(2)(b). A Magistrate has no such power, so his extension order is invalid. If the accused applies for default bail after 90 days and before the charge-sheet is filed, the right to default bail is complete. A later charge-sheet, or a wrong rejection of the application, does not defeat it.

Ramesh Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2023)
U.N. Gupta @ Udhav Narayan Gupta v. State of Bihar (2024)

N05.code: BNSS applies: the case was registered last year (2025), after 1 July 2024, so bail is under s.483 BNSS (old s.439 CrPC). If the conduct was after 1 July 2024, the offences are BNS s.318(4) (cheating) and s.316 (criminal breach of trust).
N05.expected_answer: Generally no. Bail conditions exist to secure the accused's presence and a fair investigation and trial, not to recover money for the complainant. The Supreme Court has repeatedly struck down conditions requiring deposit of the disputed amount, holding that a criminal court granting bail is not a recovery agent. Bail must be decided on the usual principles (nature of the accusation, risk of absconding or tampering), and any condition must be reasonable and connected to those aims.
N05.how_verified: Read judgment text (Dilip Singh order text). Ramesh Kumar and U.N. Gupta through secondary reports only.
N05.other_acceptable: Ramesh Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), 2023 INSC 596 (monetary deposit condition set aside); U.N. Gupta @ Udhav Narayan Gupta v. State of Bihar, SC, 2024 (courts not recovery agents; 25% deposit condition set aside)

N06.code: SC/ST Act s.3(1)(r)/(s) and s.18 apply whatever the date. Anticipatory bail is under BNSS s.482 for an FIR registered from 1 July 2024, and CrPC s.438 before that. Any accompanying general offences (insult, intimidation) are BNS s.352/351 or IPC s.504/506 depending on the date of the incident.
N06.expected_answer: No. The bar on anticipatory bail in s.18 of the SC/ST Act applies only where the complaint, read as a whole, prima facie discloses an offence under that Act. For intentional insult under s.3(1)(r), the insult must be in a place 'within public view'. It must also be meant to humiliate the person because of his caste, not merely because of a private quarrel. Abuse inside a house with only the complainant's family present is not in public view. Where these ingredients are missing, the court can consider anticipatory bail normally.
N06.how_verified: Read judgment text (Shajan Skaria judgment PDF). Hitesh Verma through a LiveLaw report.
N06.neighbour_regime: Ordinary insult and intimidation (IPC 504/506, BNS 352/351) and ordinary anticipatory bail rules (CrPC 438 / BNSS 482)

N07.code: NI Act s.138 applies whatever the date. Complaint procedure is under the BNSS if the complaint is filed from 1 July 2024, and under the CrPC before.
N07.expected_answer: Yes, it can. A cheque given 'as security' is not automatically outside s.138 NI Act. If the loan had become due on the agreed date and was not repaid, the cheque was presented for a legally enforceable debt. Its dishonour, followed by a valid notice and non-payment within 15 days, attracts s.138. Whether the debt was in fact due, or had already been repaid, is a defence to be proved at trial. It is different where the cheque secured a payment that never became due (for example, an advance against an order later cancelled).
N07.neighbour_regime: Cheating (IPC 420 / BNS 318(4)) and civil recovery of a loan
N07.older_ruling: None known (Indus Airways is a distinguishable fact pattern, not an overruled ruling).
N07.other_acceptable: Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao v. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd., (2016) 10 SCC 458 (debt existing on date of cheque: s.138 applies); Womb Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. v. authorities.label: Yogendra Pratap Singh v. Savitri Pandey (2014)
Sarav Investment v. Llyods Register of Shipping (2007)

N08.code: NI Act s.138/142 applies whatever the date. Complaint procedure is under the CrPC for a complaint filed before 1 July 2024 (as here) and the BNSS after.
N08.expected_answer: No. Under s.138(c) and s.142(b) NI Act, the cause of action arises only when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice. A complaint filed before those 15 days end is no complaint in law. Cognizance cannot be taken on it, even if the 15 days have passed by the date of cognizance. The complainant's remedy is a fresh complaint. Where an earlier complaint fails on this ground, the delay in filing the fresh complaint can be condoned under the proviso to s.142(b). Here the drawer's 15 days ran to 18 April, so a complaint filed on 10 April was premature.
N08.how_verified: Read judgment text (SC judgment copy hosted on the Rajasthan High Court site).
N08.older_ruling: OLDER RULING: Narsingh Das Tapadia v. Goverdhan Das Partani, (2000) 7 SCC 183, Supreme Court, 2000. CHANGE: Yogendra Pratap Singh v. Savitri Pandey, 3-judge bench, 2014. WHAT CHANGED: Narsingh Das Tapadia held that a premature complaint becomes maintainable if cognizance is taken after the 15 days expire; Yogendra Pratap Singh overruled it on that point and held such a complaint is not maintainable at all. CURRENT AUTHORITY: Yogendra Pratap Singh (2014).
N08.other_acceptable: Sarav Investment & Financial Consultancy (P) Ltd. v. Llyods Register of Shipping, (2007) 14 SCC 753 (approved in Yogendra Pratap Singh)

N09.code: NI Act s.138 and General Clauses Act s.27 apply whatever the date. Complaint procedure is under the BNSS for complaints filed from 1 July 2024 (old CrPC before).
N09.expected_answer: Yes. A notice sent by registered post to the drawer's correct address is presumed served under s.27 of the General Clauses Act, unless the drawer proves he did not receive it and was not responsible for that. A return marked 'unclaimed' or 'refused' does not defeat the complaint. A drawer who says he never got the notice can pay the cheque amount within 15 days of receiving the court summons with the complaint. If he does not pay, he cannot then argue that the notice was not served.

N10.code: NDPS Act and its quantity notification apply whatever the date. No IPC/BNS issue.
N10.expected_answer: The whole mixture counts. Where a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance is seized mixed with one or more neutral substances, the neutral substance is not excluded. The total weight of the mixture, together with the actual drug content, decides whether the quantity is small, intermediate or commercial (Note 4 of the 2001 notification, inserted in 2009, upheld). The older view that only the pure drug content counts is no longer good law.

Union of India, 3-judge bench, 22 Apr 2020. WHAT CHANGED: E. Micheal Raj held that only the actual content of the narcotic drug in a mixture counts; Hira Singh held that view 'is not a good law' and that neutral substances count with the drug. CURRENT AUTHORITY: Hira Singh (2020).
N10.other_acceptable: No other acceptable authority found beyond the connected matters decided with Hira Singh. Confirmed: no separate Supreme Court judgment decides this point independently.

N11.code: NDPS Act s.35/54 apply whatever the date. Burden-of-proof background: Evidence Act s.106 before 1 July 2024, BSA s.109 after.
N11.expected_answer: Not automatically. The prosecution must first prove that each accused was in possession, meaning knowledge of and control over the drugs (conscious possession). Once those basic facts are shown, the NDPS Act presumes a culpable mental state and possession (s.35 and s.54), and the accused must show, on a preponderance of probability, that he did not know. Occupants of a private car travelling together who knew each other have been held in conscious possession. A passenger with no proven link or knowledge has been acquitted.

N13.code: IPC s.420 applies because the FIR is registered under the IPC, meaning the alleged inducement was before 1 July 2024. For conduct from 1 July 2024 it would be BNS s.318(4). Quashing is under BNSS s.528 (old CrPC s.482).
N13.expected_answer: No, not by itself. Cheating needs a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time the promise or representation was made, which induced the friend to part with the money. A later failure to repay a loan, or the dishonour of a cheque given for it, is at most a breach of contract and a civil wrong. The dishonour has its own remedy under s.138 NI Act. A cheating FIR resting only on non-repayment, with nothing showing deceit at the start, is liable to be quashed.

authorities.label: Sharat Babu Digumarti v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi (2016)

N14.code: IPC s.292 and IT Act s.67 apply because the forward was in 2023, before 1 July 2024. For conduct from 1 July 2024, BNS s.294 now expressly covers 'content in electronic form', which may change the special-versus-general analysis; that is untested.
N14.expected_answer: Generally no. Where obscene material is in electronic form, the specific offence under s.67 of the IT Act applies. That Act is a special law with overriding effect (s.81), so the same act cannot also be prosecuted as obscenity under the general penal code (IPC s.292). Once the accused is discharged of the IT Act charge for that act, he cannot be proceeded against under s.292 for it. The rule covers the same act only; distinct offences with different ingredients can still be charged.

N15.code: PWDVA s.12, 20 and 23 apply whatever the date. The interim maintenance power is under s.23 read with s.20. Ordinary maintenance under CrPC 125 / BNSS 144 is a parallel but separate remedy; this question is specifically about PWDVA relief during the DV case.
N15.expected_answer: Yes. Under s.20 of the PWDVA, a Magistrate can grant interim monetary relief at any stage of the proceedings, including before a final order under s.12. This can cover maintenance, rent, medical expenses and loss of earnings. The Supreme Court has laid down guidelines for fixing interim maintenance to ensure that the dependent spouse is not left without support during litigation. The Magistrate must consider both parties' income and liabilities and fix a sum that is just and reasonable without waiting for the final disposal.
